acceptable.choice: Stay on Python/Django and fix the I/O-bound concurrency model first
acceptable.why: The requests are I/O-bound and queue behind blocked sync workers, so the problem is the concurrency model, not the language, and the team's Django skills stay fully usable.

acceptable.choice: Call the recommendations (80 ms) and pricing (40 ms) services concurrently instead of one after the other
acceptable.why: If the calls are independent, running them in parallel cuts per-request wall time by about 40 ms and shortens how long each worker is held.

acceptable.choice: Gunicorn gthread workers (threads per worker), sized against the Postgres connection limit
acceptable.why: A config-level change that lets each pod overlap many I/O waits with almost no code change, which is the cheapest first experiment.

acceptable.choice: Gunicorn with gevent workers (and psycogreen/gevent-compatible DB driver)
acceptable.why: Gives high concurrency for I/O-bound sync Django code with little rewriting, provided libraries are monkeypatch-safe.

acceptable.choice: Incremental migration of hot storefront endpoints to async Django views (ASGI on uvicorn/gunicorn+uvicorn workers) with httpx for outbound calls
acceptable.why: Native async lets one process handle many in-flight requests and run the downstream calls concurrently, while keeping the same framework and team skills.

acceptable.choice: Autoscale on concurrency/queue depth or latency (e.g., in-flight requests via KEDA or custom metrics HPA) instead of CPU
acceptable.why: CPU stays low while requests queue, so a CPU-based HPA scales on the wrong signal and leaves pods both over-provisioned and saturated.

acceptable.choice: Right-size pod CPU/memory requests and reduce pod count once per-pod concurrency rises
acceptable.why: This is where the hosting savings actually come from: fewer, better-utilized pods instead of 40 mostly idle ones.

acceptable.choice: Caching of recommendations/pricing responses and hot queries (Redis/in-process with short TTLs)
acceptable.why: Removes downstream waits from many requests entirely, which helps both p99 and capacity if staleness rules allow.

acceptable.choice: Timeouts, budgets, and graceful degradation for the recommendations call (e.g., render without recs if over ~100 ms)
acceptable.why: Recommendations are non-critical for a storefront response, so capping their tail protects the 300 ms p99 budget.

acceptable.choice: Postgres connection pooling (PgBouncer or Django 5.1+ native pool) and query optimization (N+1, indexes)
acceptable.why: More concurrency per pod raises the connection count, and DB time is a large share of each request.

ruled_out.choice: Full rewrite of the storefront API in Go
ruled_out.why: The workload is I/O-bound, so Go's CPU speed buys little. A rewrite takes many months for a 20-person Python/Django team, adds operational risk, and the latency and cost gains can be had in Python with much less effort.

ruled_out.choice: Adding more pods / raising HPA replica floor to absorb peak
ruled_out.why: It treats the symptom and makes the hosting bill, already growing faster than revenue, worse.

ruled_out.choice: Simply raising the number of sync gunicorn workers per pod without checking memory or DB connections
ruled_out.why: Each sync worker is a full process, so this burns memory and Postgres connections linearly and is a costly half-measure compared with threads, gevent, or async.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting in another language or framework for speed (Rust, Node, FastAPI rewrite) as the primary fix
ruled_out.why: Same problem as Go: a big migration cost aimed at CPU throughput, which is not the bottleneck.

ruled_out.choice: Vertical scaling to bigger nodes / more CPU per pod
ruled_out.why: CPU is already underused, so more CPU fixes nothing and costs more.

ruled_out.choice: Moving the downstream calls into Celery tasks on the request path
ruled_out.why: Celery is for background work. Waiting synchronously on task results adds broker latency and still blocks the worker.

must_mention: The bottleneck is I/O wait with sync workers (concurrency per pod), not CPU or language speed, so moving to Go is not the necessary fix
Queueing at peak is what drives p99 from about 300 ms to 900 ms, and raising per-pod concurrency (threads, gevent, or async) attacks it directly
Parallelize the independent recommendations and pricing calls (and add timeouts/fallbacks), because serial downstream waits are a fixed latency floor
Scaling on CPU is the wrong signal for this workload; scale on in-flight requests, queue depth, or latency
Cost savings come from higher utilization per pod, which allows fewer pods and right-sized requests, not from a faster language
Higher concurrency raises Postgres connection pressure, so pooling (PgBouncer or the native pool) and DB tuning must come with it
Measure first: profile or trace a request's time breakdown and peak queue time before and after changes
Give leadership a direct answer: Go is unlikely to pay off here compared with fixing the concurrency model in the existing stack
red_flags: Recommending a Go rewrite as the main answer, or claiming Go will cut costs by some large factor, without addressing that the workload is I/O-bound
Recommending more pods, bigger nodes, or more CPU as the fix
Claiming Python is inherently too slow, or blaming the GIL for this I/O-bound problem

Recommending gevent, threads, or async without warning about Postgres connection exhaustion or blocking/non-cooperative libraries (e.g., sync ORM calls inside async views without sync_to_async, C extensions under gevent)
Saying async Django is a drop-in switch, while ignoring that the ORM's async support is partial, middleware must be async-compatible, and sync code in async views blocks the event loop
Proposing a big-bang migration without incremental rollout, load testing, or before/after p99 and cost measurement
Suggesting the downstream calls be made asynchronous through Celery on the request path
unknowns: Whether the recommendations and pricing calls are independent (can run in parallel) or one needs the other's output
The actual per-request time breakdown (DB vs. downstream vs. CPU/serialization) and how much of p99 is queue wait vs. service time
Current gunicorn worker count per pod, pod resource requests/limits, and memory per worker
How much of the hosting bill is the storefront pods vs. Postgres, Celery workers, the downstream services, egress, or other items (the API may not be the main cost driver)
Postgres max connections, whether a pooler exists, and how much headroom the DB has for more concurrent queries
Whether the libraries in use (DB driver, HTTP clients, SDKs) are gevent/async-safe
Tolerated staleness for recommendations and pricing, which decides how much caching is allowed
Whether the recommendations and pricing services can absorb the higher concurrent load once callers stop being throttled by sync workers
Django version (affects native async ORM coverage and built-in connection pooling)
